facts: Aconcagua, in the Argentine Andes, is the highest mountain outside Asia at 6,961 metres, and the highest point in both the Western and Southern hemispheres.
Argentina stretches from subtropical forest in the north to the sub-Antarctic tip of Tierra del Fuego.
Its border with Chile, running along the Andes, is the third longest international border in the world.
Bolivia has two capitals: Sucre is the constitutional seat and La Paz holds the government.
The Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat in the world and holds a large share of global lithium reserves.
It lost its coastline to Chile in the 19th century and still maintains a navy on Lake Titicaca.
Brazil borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.
It holds about 60% of the Amazon rainforest and the largest river by discharge in the world.
Brasília was built from nothing in the 1950s and inaugurated as the capital in 1960.
Chile runs over 4,300 kilometres north to south but averages under 180 kilometres wide.
The Atacama Desert is the driest non-polar place on Earth, with some weather stations never recording rain.
Ojos del Salado is the highest active volcano in the world.
Colombia is the only South American country with coastlines on both the Pacific and the Caribbean.
It is the second most biodiverse country in the world and has more bird species than any other.
The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta rises to 5,700 metres within 50 kilometres of the sea.
Because of the equatorial bulge, Chimborazo's summit is the farthest point on the surface from the Earth's centre.
Ecuador was the first country to write rights of nature into its constitution, in 2008.
The Galápagos Islands, roughly 1,000 kilometres offshore, shaped Darwin's theory of natural selection.
Guyana is the only South American country with English as its official language.
Kaieteur Falls drops 226 metres in a single uninterrupted plunge, roughly four times the height of Niagara.
Large offshore oil discoveries after 2015 made it one of the fastest-growing economies in the world.
Paraguay is one of only two landlocked countries in South America, along with Bolivia.
The Itaipú Dam, shared with Brazil, is among the largest hydroelectric plants in the world and supplies most of Paraguay's power.
Guaraní is an official language alongside Spanish and is spoken by most of the population.
Machu Picchu, built in the 15th century, was never found by the Spanish and stayed largely unknown outside the region until 1911.
Peru shares Lake Titicaca with Bolivia, the highest navigable lake in the world.
The potato was domesticated in the Peruvian Andes, where thousands of varieties are still grown.
Suriname is the smallest sovereign state in South America, both by land area and by population.
Dutch is the official language, the only country in the Americas where that is the case.
More than 90% of the country is still covered by rainforest.
Uruguay generates the large majority of its electricity from renewable sources, chiefly wind and hydro.
It won the first FIFA World Cup, hosted at home in 1930.
Roughly half the national population lives in the Montevideo metropolitan area.
Angel Falls drops 979 metres, the tallest uninterrupted waterfall in the world.
Venezuela holds the largest proven oil reserves of any country.
Lake Maracaibo sees near-nightly lightning storms, among the most frequent anywhere on Earth.
